item.question: Find the perimeter of an equilateral triangle ABC in terms of the length of one side.
steps: The perimeter of any triangle is the sum of its three sides: AB + BC + AC.
All three sides are equal, so AB + BC + AC = AB + AB + AB.
Three copies of AB make 3 × AB.
item.answer: 3 × the length of a side.

item.question: What is a similarity between a square and an equilateral triangle?
steps: A square has four equal sides and four equal angles.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles.
Both have all sides equal and all angles equal, so both are regular polygons. That is why both perimeters are the number of sides × one side.
item.answer: Both are regular: all sides equal and all angles equal, so both use the number of sides × one side.

item.question: Akshi says the perimeter of the triangle on the dot grid is 9 units. Toshi says it cannot be 9 units and will be more than 9 units. Who is right?
steps_tex: Count the edges: six go straight across or straight up and down, and three slant.
Lay one straight unit on one slanted unit. It falls short, so a slanted unit is longer than a straight unit.
So the nine edges are not nine equal units. The perimeter is $6$ straight units plus $3$ diagonal units, written $6s + 3d$.
Three of the nine edges are longer than one straight unit, so the perimeter is more than $9\text{ units}$. Toshi is right.

item.question: Find the perimeter of other regular polygons, and write a rule for the perimeter of any regular polygon.
steps_tex: A regular pentagon has $5$ equal sides, so its perimeter is $5 \times$ one side. A regular hexagon has $6$ equal sides, so its perimeter is $6 \times$ one side.
A regular hexagon with each side $5\text{ cm}$ has a perimeter of $6 \times 5 = 30\text{ cm}$.
The pattern is the same for every regular polygon: write one side as many times as there are sides.

item.question: The chit, 6 cm by 4 cm, is cut into two equal pieces. The pieces are joined end to end along their 2 cm edges. What is the perimeter of this long strip?
steps: Each piece is 6 cm by 2 cm, so each has a perimeter of 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm.
The two pieces touch along a 2 cm edge. That edge is lost from each piece, so 2 cm + 2 cm = 4 cm leaves the boundary.
16 + 16 - 2 - 2 = 28 cm. The strip is 12 cm by 2 cm, and 2 × (12 + 2) = 28 cm agrees.
item.answer: 28 cm

$2$. Their areas are $2 \times 4 = 8\text{ sq m}$, $1 \times 6 = 6\text{ sq m}$, $2 \times 3 = 6\text{ sq m}$ and $2 \times 4 = 8\text{ sq m}$.
$3$. Add the pieces: $8 + 6 + 6 + 8 = 28\text{ sq m}$.
$4$. Figure $b$ is a top bar with two legs. The top bar is $5\text{ m}$ by $1\text{ m}$ and each leg is $1\text{ m}$ by $2\text{ m}$.
$5$. Their areas are $5 \times 1 = 5\text{ sq m}$, $1 \times 2 = 2\text{ sq m}$ and $1 \times 2 = 2\text{ sq m}$. Add them: $5 + 2 + 2 = 9\text{ sq m}$.
Answer: $(a)$: $28\text{ sq m}$, $(b)$: $9\text{ sq m}$.

item.question: Look at the two figures, a curved one and a spiky one. Guess which of them has the larger area.
steps: A guess made by looking is only a first idea, because the two shapes have very different edges.
To settle it, trace each figure onto squared paper and count its squares with the four rules.
The shape with the greater count in square units has the larger area.
item.answer: A guess, settled by counting squares.

item.question: What are the four rules for counting squares to estimate an area on squared paper?
item.answer: A full square is 1 square unit; a part more than half a square counts as 1; a part less than half is ignored; exactly half a square counts as 1/2.

item.question: Draw a circle of diameter 3 on a graph sheet. Count the squares and use them to estimate the area of the circular region.
steps: Draw the circle with a width of 3 squares, then count the squares that are whole inside it.
Look at each square on the edge. Count it as 1 if more than half of it is inside, ignore it if less than half is inside, and count it as 1/2 if exactly half is inside.
Add the whole squares and the edge squares that you counted. The area comes to about 7 square units.
item.answer: About 7 square units, found with the half-square rule.

item.question: Why can we not use circles instead of squares to find the area?
steps: Pack a rectangle with circles. There are gaps between the circles, so the circles do not cover the whole rectangle.
Pack the same rectangle in another way. The first packing holds 42 circles and the second holds 44, so one rectangle gives two different counts.
Squares fit edge to edge with no gaps and no overlaps, so the count of squares is the same every time.
item.answer: Circles leave gaps, so the count changes with the packing; squares tile with no gaps and no overlaps.

item.question: Find the area of the four figures drawn on the grid of dots.
steps_tex: The first figure has $3$ whole squares and $2$ squares that are exactly half: $3 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 4$ square units.
The second figure has $6$ whole squares and $6$ half squares: $6 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 9$ square units.
The third figure has $7$ whole squares and $6$ half squares: $7 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 10$ square units.
The fourth figure has $8$ whole squares and $6$ half squares: $8 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 11$ square units.
